title: Google Pauses Open-Source Bug Bounty Over Flood of AI-Generated 'Slop' Reports
excerpt: Google stopped accepting new product vulnerability reports to its OSS VRP on October 1, saying a "significant rise in automated submissions" — mostly AI-generated and invalid — had overwhelmed maintainers.
body:
• Google's Open Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program (OSS VRP) stopped accepting new product vulnerability reports on October 1, 2026, citing "a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid."
  • The freeze is narrower than the headlines suggest: supply-chain reports, reports filed before October 1, and some Google Cloud repository reports remain unaffected.
  • Google has promised an update on the program's future in Q1 2027, with no commitment to reopen it in its current form.
  • The move reflects a structural problem for the industry: AI-generated "slop" is overwhelming human triage across bug-bounty programs, with Intel pausing its own program for similar reasons.

Google has frozen its open-source bug bounty program for product vulnerabilities, saying it has been overwhelmed by a flood of low-quality, AI-generated submissions. As of October 1, 2026, the company's Open Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program (OSS VRP) is no longer accepting new product vulnerability reports — a decision announced on X and the program's website, and first reported widely by TechCrunch on October 4.

The pause

The OSS VRP paid independent researchers for finding vulnerabilities in Google's open-source software, and had become a steady source of bug-bounty income for security researchers worldwide. Google's announcement was blunt about the reason for the shutdown:

https://x.com/CharlesChong96/status/2106906616058511656

"As of October 1, 2026, we are no longer accepting product vulnerabilities submitted to the OSS VRP. This pause is due to a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which are not valid. We will continue to reformat and work on this aspect of the OSS VRP and commit to giving an update in Q1 2027."

— Google, OSS VRP program announcement

Researchers who filed reports before October 1 will still have them processed, and the company steered hunters toward its other programs — including the main Google VRP and the Patch Rewards Program, which pays for security patches to open-source projects rather than just vulnerability reports.

Why AI "slop" broke the system

The problem is not AI finding real bugs — it is AI flooding triage queues with ones that are not. Security researchers describe a wave of low-effort reports: claimed vulnerabilities that turn out to be ordinary coding errors with no security impact, or in some cases entirely hallucinated flaws. Each one still requires a human to validate, and maintainers were being buried.

As TechCrunch noted, cybersecurity experts warned in 2025 that "AI slop posed a serious risk to bug bounty programs." That warning has now materialized. Secondary reporting points to Linux maintainers being "completely overwhelmed," with some release cycles seeing as many as 2,000 reported CVEs — and Intel having already paused its own bounty, which paid up to $100,000 per flaw, over similar submission-quality concerns. Google has not published its own submission-volume figures, so the scale of the flood inside its program remains undisclosed.

What stays open

The freeze covers only product vulnerability reports. Supply-chain reports — covering compromised build pipelines and tampered packages — are unaffected. For some Google Cloud repositories that touch Cloud products, researchers can still submit through the separate Cloud VRP. In practice, Google is keeping the doors open where the signal-to-noise ratio is still manageable, and closing the one where AI submissions have made triage untenable.

Diaspora angle

India is one of the largest sources of independent security researchers in the world, and Indian hunters have been regular earners across Google's bounty programs. The freeze closes one well-trodden path for open-source-focused researchers — but the Patch Rewards Program and the main VRP remain open, so the message is narrower: the bar for getting paid has moved up, not disappeared. For the growing community of Indian security researchers, the profitable hunt now favors demonstrably real, high-impact flaws over volume submissions.

What's next

Google says it will "reformat" the program and give an update in the first quarter of 2027 — language that leaves room for a redesigned program with different submission processes or payment structures, as Neowin has speculated. The bigger question is structural: AI has made generating bug reports nearly free, and until AI-assisted triage can match AI-assisted submissions, every bounty program in the industry faces the same math Google just ran.
